Eleven directions for a mark that has to be the friendliest thing in the waiting room

A logo concept review for Pediatric Ear, Nose & Throat Specialists: eleven new treatments of the bunny, the elephant and the giraffe, from a light refresh to a full redraw, shown beside the mark you use today.
Concept Review Round 01 · September 2026
Where we are today

The mark you use now

Before anything new, the baseline. This is the logo currently on the site, the signage and the paperwork, and it is the thing every concept in this round has to beat.

Current mark · shown at the full size of the file we were given: 355 × 111 pixels
How to use this page

Eleven marks. Three characters. One decision.

Each concept is numbered. You do not need to agree internally before replying — reply with the numbers that stop you, and tell us which ones your front desk and your clinical staff each gravitate toward. A split vote is useful information, not a problem.

How to read these

Four questions worth asking of every option

A logo that only works at the top of a website is only half a logo. These are the four tests we apply before recommending anything, and they are worth holding each concept up against as you scroll.

  • Does it still read at 32 pixels? Your mark lives in a browser tab, a phone app icon and the corner of a referral fax at least as often as it lives on the building.
  • Does it survive one color? Embroidery on scrubs, a stamp on a sticker chart, a single-color form header. Some uses have no palette at all.
  • Can the animals leave home? A concept whose characters hold up on their own gives you a mascot set for signage, forms and the Learning Center, not just a header graphic.
  • Does it feel like your practice? The honest test: put it next to the last three pediatric offices you visited. Does it look like yours, or like a stock icon set anyone could have bought?

The concepts

Eleven directions, in no particular order

These are presented flat and unranked on purpose. We have opinions and we will share them once you have reacted — but a first read that is not steered tells us more about where this brand should go than our shortlist does. They run from 01, a close cousin of what you have, through 10, which is closer to children's-book illustration, to 11, which keeps your existing colors outright.

01

Open Span

Flat silhouette · Bookend lockup
Composition

Closest to the mark you use today. Bunny left, giraffe right, elephant lifted above the name — the same architecture, redrawn with rounder forms.

Palette

Taupe elephant, dusty mauve bunny, sage giraffe. The quietest set in the round.

Strongest use

A drop-in replacement. Website header, letterhead and signage all keep the proportions you already build around.

02

Parade

Flat silhouette · Stacked lockup
Composition

Three animals in a row, all facing the same way, above a centered two-line setting of the name. Reads as a procession rather than a group portrait.

Palette

Peach, soft teal, lilac — the widest hue spread of the stacked options.

Strongest use

Square and vertical spaces: app icon, social avatar, the top of a portrait-format intake form.

03

Family Group

Flat silhouette · Left cluster
Composition

The three drawn as one shape — giraffe leaning over the elephant, bunny tucked in front — set to the left of the name.

Palette

Sage, periwinkle, blush. The softest and most muted grouping here.

Strongest use

Wide horizontal placements: site header, email signature, the spine of a folder, a vehicle door.

04

Badge Set

Illustrated portraits · Badge system
Composition

Each animal gets its own circular badge and a full face rather than a silhouette, with the name centered underneath.

Palette

Sage, lavender and peach circles behind cream and lilac characters.

Strongest use

The most modular option in the round — three ready-made icons for departments, forms, wayfinding and the Learning Center, not just a header.

05

Linework

Single-weight outline · Stacked lockup
Composition

Outline drawings at one stroke weight, above a centered name. The lightest mark in the round by a wide margin.

Palette

Sage, plum and tan carried in the line itself rather than in a fill.

Strongest use

Print, foil, embossing and anywhere a solid shape would feel heavy. Also the easiest of the ten to animate, since the line can draw itself on.

06

Row

Flat silhouette · Stacked lockup
Composition

Flat silhouettes at a larger scale, evenly spaced above the name. The most confident of the stacked layouts.

Palette

Dusty rose, mint and periwinkle — the coolest, calmest set.

Strongest use

Anywhere the mark is the main event: building signage, scrub embroidery, the cover of a new-patient packet.

07

Overlap Cluster

Flat silhouette · Left cluster
Composition

The three overlapping — giraffe behind, elephant center, bunny in front — set left of the name. The tightest grouping in the round.

Palette

Soft teal, lilac and terracotta. The warmest cool pairing of the ten.

Strongest use

Horizontal headers and any placement with more width than height.

08

Wide Span

Flat silhouette · Bookend lockup
Composition

The bookend structure of the current mark with a wider stance: bunny far left, giraffe far right, elephant raised above the name.

Palette

Peach, sage and lilac — the most evenly balanced three-hue set here.

Strongest use

Wide, short spaces: a site header, an email banner, the top of a billboard-format ad.

09

Peek

Cropped portraits · Stacked lockup
Composition

Faces only, cropped as though the three are looking over the top of the name. The most character-forward option in the round.

Palette

Peach, soft teal and lilac — the warmest set of the ten.

Strongest use

Screens and social, where personality matters more than formality. The elephant alone would make a strong app icon.

10

Illustrated Family

Rendered illustration · Left cluster
Composition

The most rendered option: modeled shading, real expressions and layered depth, grouped to the left of the name.

Palette

Mauve, tan and sage, with a deeper brown carrying the giraffe's spots and hooves.

Strongest use

Storybook applications — a coloring sheet, a wall mural, a what-to-expect-before-surgery booklet for kids.

11

Primary Refresh

Flat silhouette · Bookend lockup · Existing palette
Composition

Your current structure and your current palette, simply redrawn: bunny left, giraffe right, elephant raised above the name. The geometry is cleaned up, the animals are redrawn as smooth shapes, and the spacing is evened out.

Palette

Unchanged — your red, yellow and blue, in slightly cleaner, deeper values. The only concept in the round that keeps them.

Strongest use

Everywhere the current mark already lives. It is the only option here that needs no website color pass and no reprint of signage or stationery already in stock.
